```{r}
#| label: setup
#| include: false

options(width = 90)
options(cli.unicode = FALSE)
pkg_root <- if (file.exists("DESCRIPTION")) {
  "."
} else if (file.exists("../DESCRIPTION")) {
  ".."
} else {
  NA_character_
}
if (!is.na(pkg_root) && requireNamespace("pkgload", quietly = TRUE)) {
  pkgload::load_all(pkg_root, quiet = TRUE)
}
default_output_hook <- knitr::knit_hooks$get("output")
knitr::knit_hooks$set(
  output = function(x, options) {
    x <- gsub(
      "Database:(\\s+)[^\\r\\n]+[.]duckdb",
      "Database:\\1<temporary DuckDB path>",
      x,
      perl = TRUE
    )
    x <- gsub("[ \t]+(?=\n)", "", x, perl = TRUE)
    default_output_hook(x, options)
  }
)

# This article starts from a sealed snapshot. Build its deterministic offline
# fixture here so every shown workflow chunk can execute without teaching data
# preparation a second time.
ids <- sprintf("DEMO_%02d", 1:8)
pit <- ledgr::ledgr_sim_pit_inputs(
  ids,
  from = "2018-01-01",
  to = "2020-12-31",
  seed = 7L
)
# Give the worked optimization one deliberately redundant asset. DEMO_08 is
# a high-beta version of DEMO_03, so the inspected long-only solution has a
# binding zero weight rather than merely satisfying inactive constraints.
leader <- pit$bars[pit$bars$instrument_id == "DEMO_03", , drop = FALSE]
leader <- leader[order(leader$ts_utc), , drop = FALSE]
follower <- which(pit$bars$instrument_id == "DEMO_08")
follower <- follower[order(pit$bars$ts_utc[follower])]
stopifnot(identical(leader$ts_utc, pit$bars$ts_utc[follower]))
leader_return <- c(0, diff(log(leader$close)))
synthetic_return <- 3 * leader_return + 0.0001 * sin(seq_along(leader_return))
synthetic_close <- pit$bars$close[follower[[1L]]] * exp(cumsum(synthetic_return))
pit$bars$open[follower] <- synthetic_close
pit$bars$high[follower] <- synthetic_close * 1.001
pit$bars$low[follower] <- synthetic_close * 0.999
pit$bars$close[follower] <- synthetic_close
facts <- ledgr::ledgr_facts(
  ledgr::ledgr_facts_sessions(
    pit$sessions,
    venue_id = "DEMO_VENUE",
    knowledge = "evidenced",
    timezone = "UTC"
  ),
  ledgr::ledgr_facts_membership_snapshots(
    pit$membership,
    universe_id = "DEMO_UNIVERSE",
    complete = TRUE,
    knowledge = "evidenced"
  ),
  ledgr::ledgr_facts_trading_status(
    pit$trading_status,
    knowledge = "evidenced"
  ),
  ledgr::ledgr_facts_lifetime(
    pit$lifetime,
    knowledge = "evidenced"
  ),
  ledgr::ledgr_facts_equity_corporate_actions(pit$corporate_actions)
)
snapshot_path <- file.path(tempdir(), "minimum-variance-demo.duckdb")
if (file.exists(snapshot_path)) unlink(snapshot_path)
built <- ledgr::ledgr_snapshot_from_df(
  pit$bars,
  instruments_df = pit$instruments,
  facts = facts,
  db_path = snapshot_path,
  snapshot_id = "minimum_variance_demo",
  price_basis = "split_adjusted"
)
ledgr::ledgr_snapshot_close(built)
```

A minimum-variance portfolio asks a precise question: among the portfolios
you permit, which one has the lowest estimated variance? This article answers
that question inside a complete ledgr strategy. You will read a causal return
matrix, check that it contains a usable sample, estimate and solve the
portfolio in ordinary R, and turn the solution into share targets.

This is the global minimum-variance portfolio: it uses estimated covariance,
not an expected-return forecast. That makes it a useful first optimization
example because the statistical input, constraints and execution intent stay
easy to see.

The complete path is:

```text
causal returns -> ready sample -> covariance -> long-only weights -> targets
```

Ledgr then applies execution and cost policy, records fills and accounting
events, and stores a reproducible result. The statistical estimate remains
ordinary R code; ledgr owns the causal input and the economic record.

The quadratic solver comes from `quadprog`; `dplyr` and `tidyr` keep the shown
result tables compact. Install them before running the article yourself:

```r
install.packages(c("quadprog", "dplyr", "tidyr"))
```

## Start From A Sealed Snapshot

This article starts where portfolio research normally starts: with a sealed
snapshot prepared by an adapter or a previous data step. Its hidden setup
builds a deterministic, offline snapshot of eight synthetic equities over
three years, including a venue calendar and point-in-time membership. Open it
like any other snapshot:

```{r}
#| label: open-snapshot
#| message: false

library(ledgr)
library(dplyr)
library(tidyr)

snapshot <- ledgr_snapshot_open(snapshot_path)
```

For the preparation workflow, read
`vignette("point-in-time-inputs", package = "ledgr")`. For the exact meaning
of a causal history window, read
`vignette("causal-history", package = "ledgr")`.

::: {.ledgr-callout .ledgr-callout-note}
**Demo data**

The snapshot is synthetic. One asset deliberately resembles a high-beta
version of another so the long-only constraint becomes visible. The example
proves the workflow, not an investment result.
:::

## State The Research Choices

The strategy has four choices. Keeping them in one visible object makes them
part of every run and sweep candidate rather than hidden constants in the
callback.

```{r}
#| label: strategy-params

strategy_params <- list(
  lookback = 252L,
  min_instruments = 2L,
  covariance_shrinkage = 0.5,
  equity_fraction = 0.95
)
```

- `lookback` is the number of expected venue sessions in the covariance
  window. Because this article does not override `min_observations`, ledgr's
  finite-lookback default admits an instrument only when all 252 return
  observations are finite.
- `min_instruments` is the minimum number of admitted instruments required
  before the strategy estimates a portfolio.
- `covariance_shrinkage` pulls the sample covariance toward its diagonal. A
  value of `0.5` gives equal weight to the sample covariance and its diagonal,
  which makes the estimate positive definite when every admitted instrument
  has positive variance.
- `equity_fraction` sizes at the decision close using 95% of available equity.
  The remaining headroom helps absorb price movement before next-open
  execution; whole-share rounding may leave additional cash.

These are example choices, not recommended universal values. Their purpose is
to make the method auditable.

## Write The Strategy

The strategy body describes one portfolio decision. A declarative schedule,
attached when the experiment is built, asks ledgr to invoke that body on the
first open session of each month. Calendar logic therefore stays out of the
portfolio method.

```{r}
#| label: strategy

min_variance <- function(ctx, params) {
  returns <- ctx |>
    ledgr_history_matrix(
      feature = "return_1",
      lookback = params$lookback,
      min_instruments = params$min_instruments
    )
  if (!ledgr_passed_warmup(returns)) {
    return(list(
      targets = ctx$hold(),
      intent_reason = "insufficient_sample"
    ))
  }

  sigma <- cov(returns)
  diagonal <- diag(diag(sigma), nrow = nrow(sigma))
  sigma <- (1 - params$covariance_shrinkage) * sigma +
    params$covariance_shrinkage * diagonal
  if (any(!is.finite(sigma)) || any(diag(sigma) <= 0)) {
    return(list(
      targets = ctx$hold(),
      intent_reason = "insufficient_sample"
    ))
  }

  n <- ncol(sigma)
  solution <- quadprog::solve.QP(
    Dmat = sigma,
    dvec = rep(0, n),
    Amat = cbind(rep(1, n), diag(n)),
    bvec = c(1, rep(0, n)),
    meq = 1L
  )$solution
  if (any(!is.finite(solution)) || any(solution < -1e-8) ||
      abs(sum(solution) - 1) > 1e-8) {
    stop("The optimizer returned invalid long-only weights.")
  }
  solution[solution < 0] <- 0
  solution <- solution / sum(solution)

  targets <- solution |>
    ledgr_align_weights(returns) |>
    ledgr_target_rebalance(
      ctx,
      equity_fraction = params$equity_fraction
    )

  # This strategy follows the point-in-time index. A holding that has left
  # the membership universe is therefore assigned a zero target.
  targets[!ctx$vec$member] <- 0

  list(targets = targets, intent_reason = "rebalanced")
}
```

There is one ordinary history read for the estimator. The returned object is
a sessions-by-instruments double matrix, so `cov()` and `quadprog` consume it
directly. `ledgr_align_weights()` restores the matrix's instrument identity to
the unnamed numerical solution; the strategy never reconstructs names from
matrix columns.

The two intent reasons are deliberately sparse. `insufficient_sample` means a
scheduled decision lacked enough usable data. `rebalanced` means the strategy
submitted a new target. On other sessions ledgr does not invoke the strategy,
and records a scheduled skip rather than a strategy hold. A genuine solver
failure is an error rather than a silent hold.

## Build The Experiment

The experiment registers the daily-return feature, the historical membership
universe and zero transaction costs. Replacing the cost model changes what the
same target intent costs; it does not change the covariance estimate.

```{r}
#| label: experiment

exp <- ledgr_experiment(
  snapshot,
  ledgr_strategy_schedule(
    min_variance,
    ledgr_schedule_month_start()
  ),
  features = list(ledgr_ind_returns(1L)),
  universe = ledgr_universe_members("DEMO_UNIVERSE"),
  cost_model = ledgr_cost_zero()
)
```

Because the strategy calls a package-qualified external solver, preflight
records `quadprog` as a dependency that sweep workers must be able to load:

```{r}
#| label: preflight

check <- ledgr_strategy_preflight(min_variance)
check$tier
check$worker_dependencies$require_namespace
```

## Inspect One Decision

`ledgr_pulse_snapshot()` is an inspection tool: it gives you the same public
context the strategy receives at one pulse without running a backtest. It is
useful here for seeing the estimator input and the resulting target together.

```{r}
#| label: one-decision
#| eval: !expr requireNamespace("quadprog", quietly = TRUE)

decision_ctx <- ledgr_pulse_snapshot(
  exp,
  ts_utc = as.Date("2019-11-01"),
  params = strategy_params
)
returns <- decision_ctx |>
  ledgr_history_matrix(
    feature = "return_1",
    lookback = strategy_params$lookback,
    min_instruments = strategy_params$min_instruments
  )
dim(returns)

decision <- min_variance(decision_ctx, strategy_params)
decision$intent_reason
decision$targets[colnames(returns)]
close(decision_ctx)
```

The matrix dimensions answer the sample question directly: rows are expected
sessions and columns are admitted instruments. The target is a full named
quantity vector over the decision axis. Ledgr will try to fill the difference
between current and target quantities at the next eligible open. See
`vignette("execution-semantics", package = "ledgr")` for that timing rule.
`DEMO_08` has a zero target: its deliberately redundant return stream makes
the long-only constraint bind rather than permitting a negative weight.

## Run And Read The Result

```{r}
#| label: run
#| eval: !expr requireNamespace("quadprog", quietly = TRUE)

bt <- exp |>
  ledgr_run(
    params = strategy_params,
    run_id = "minimum-variance"
  )

fill_days <- ledgr_results(bt, "fills") |>
  distinct(fill_day = as.Date(ts_utc))
nrow(fill_days)
slice_head(fill_days, n = 4L)
bt
```

The first year supplies the 252-session sample, so the strategy records
`insufficient_sample` on early monthly decisions and begins trading once the
panel is ready. Each fill occurs on the session after its decision because the
experiment uses ledgr's next-open execution convention.

The result also reports costs, corporate-action fidelity, valuation status,
returns and drawdown. Those are ledger outputs, not values recomputed by the
strategy.

## Why The Optimization Has This Shape

The objective is `minimize w' Sigma w`, subject to `sum(w) = 1` and
`w_i >= 0` for every instrument.

The first constraint invests the allocated capital. The second makes the
portfolio long-only. They appear in `solve.QP()` as one equality column and
one non-negativity column per instrument.

The diagonal shrinkage is part of the estimator, not a ledgr requirement. It
stabilizes a covariance matrix when the number of instruments is large
relative to the window. This article uses a fixed shrinkage value so the
portfolio workflow stays visible; production research should choose and
validate that value out of sample.

## Sweep One Research Choice

An ordinary data frame gives one candidate per row. Here only the shrinkage
strength changes; the other choices remain visible rather than being merged
from hidden defaults.

```{r}
#| label: sweep
#| eval: !expr requireNamespace("quadprog", quietly = TRUE)

grid <- data.frame(
  lookback = rep(252L, 3L),
  min_instruments = rep(2L, 3L),
  covariance_shrinkage = c(0.25, 0.50, 0.75),
  equity_fraction = rep(0.95, 3L)
)

sweep <- ledgr_sweep(exp, grid, seed = 1L)
sweep |>
  as_tibble() |>
  unnest_wider(params) |>
  select(
    candidate_id,
    covariance_shrinkage,
    status,
    sharpe_ratio,
    total_return,
    max_drawdown
  )
```

The compact view puts the changed shrinkage value beside each candidate ID and
its main outcomes. This is exploration, not validation: choosing a shrinkage
value from the same period used to report it would overstate the evidence. For
held-out evaluation, continue with
`vignette("walk-forward", package = "ledgr")`.

::: {.ledgr-callout .ledgr-callout-tip}
**Try it**

Which shrinkage value has the highest in-sample Sharpe ratio in the compact
table? Replace the three `lookback` values with `126L` and rerun the sweep.
Does the ranking change, and why would neither ranking by itself validate the
choice?
:::

## What This Article Deliberately Leaves Elsewhere

This strategy excludes an instrument until its return window is complete and
assigns zero to an eligible instrument omitted from the allocation. More
advanced choices—keeping an omitted holding, turnover-aware optimization,
no-trade bands and richer allocation diagnostics—are deliberately outside
this introductory method.

Carried observations and missing-session evidence are taught in
`vignette("causal-history", package = "ledgr")`. Liquidity and capacity are a
different question again: whether an intended quantity could realistically
trade. They belong to execution policy, not to this covariance example; see
`vignette("risk-and-cost", package = "ledgr")` for that boundary.
